_about: Deep Dives: rare bonus cards. Landing on one shows a RARE FIND banner; after the guess, a Deep Dive button opens these in-depth facts. Keyed by card id. Each fact: [label, text], kid-friendly, 180 characters max.
_verify: Written from memory on 2026-11-19. Fact-check before launch.

lake-superior.tagline: The giant of the Great Lakes
facts: World record
Lake Superior is the biggest freshwater lake on Earth by surface area. It's almost as big as the whole state of Maine!
Fresh water
It holds about 10% of all the fresh water sitting on Earth's surface.
Where it is
It touches three US states, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan, and the Canadian province of Ontario.
Super deep
Its deepest spot is about 1,333 feet down, deeper than the Eiffel Tower is tall.
Its first name
The Ojibwe people call it Gichigami, which means 'great sea.'
History
In the 1600s and 1700s, French voyageurs paddled giant birch-bark canoes across it, carrying beaver furs to trade.
What ships carry
Today, 1,000-foot ships called 'lakers' carry iron ore from Minnesota's mines across the lake to make steel.
The Soo Locks
At the Soo Locks, giant water elevators lift and lower ships about 21 feet between Lake Superior and Lake Huron.
Wild island
Isle Royale, a national park out in the lake, is famous for its moose and wolves.
Brrr
Deep down, its water stays about 39°F all year round.

lake-michigan.tagline: Big cities, giant dunes and a backwards river
facts: Where it is
Lake Michigan touches four states: Michigan, Indiana, Illinois and Wisconsin.
Big cities
Chicago and Milwaukee both sit right on its shores.
Secret twin
Lake Michigan and Lake Huron are joined by a wide strait, so scientists say they're really one giant lake: Michigan-Huron.
Mighty bridge
The Mackinac Bridge stretches about 5 miles across the strait between the two lakes.
No cars allowed
On Mackinac Island, cars are banned. People get around by bike, on foot and by horse, and the island is famous for fudge.
How Chicago grew
In the 1800s, ships carried grain, lumber and goods across the lake, and a canal linked it to the Mississippi. Chicago boomed into a giant city.
A backwards river
In 1900, engineers made the Chicago River flow backward, away from the lake, to keep the lake's water clean.
Dunes
Indiana Dunes National Park sits on its southern shore, with sandy hills and beaches.
Its name
Its name likely comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great water.'

lake-huron.tagline: The lake with the longest shoreline
facts: Where it is
Lake Huron touches the state of Michigan and the Canadian province of Ontario.
First seen
It was the first Great Lake that European explorers saw, when Samuel de Champlain arrived in 1615.
Its name
French explorers named it after the Huron, or Wendat, people who lived along its shores.
Longest shore
Counting all its islands, Lake Huron has the longest shoreline of any of the Great Lakes.
The sixth Great Lake
Georgian Bay, part of Lake Huron, is so big that people nickname it the 'sixth Great Lake.'
Rock pillars
Flowerpot Island has tall rock towers shaped like giant flowerpots, carved by waves over thousands of years.
What ships carry
Ships carry iron ore, grain and limestone across it. Michigan's shore has one of the biggest limestone quarries in the world.
Underwater museum
Thunder Bay Marine Sanctuary protects nearly 100 historic shipwrecks that divers can explore.
Twin lake
It's connected to Lake Michigan by a wide strait, and both lakes sit at the same water level.

lake-erie.tagline: Canals, roller coasters and Niagara Falls
facts: Where it is
Lake Erie touches four states, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York, plus Ontario in Canada.
The Erie Canal
In 1825, the Erie Canal linked Lake Erie to the Hudson River and New York City. Boats carried grain east and goods west, and New York boomed.
Niagara Falls
Lake Erie's water flows down the Niagara River and pours over Niagara Falls on its way to Lake Ontario.
Fishing
Lake Erie is famous for walleye, a tasty fish, and has more fish than any other Great Lake.
Coaster capital
Cedar Point, one of the world's most famous roller coaster parks, sits on a peninsula in Lake Erie.
Rock and roll
Cleveland's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame stands right on the lake's shore.
Frozen lake
Because it's so shallow, Lake Erie often freezes almost all the way across in winter.
Its name
It's named after the Erie people. Their name is often translated as 'long tail,' maybe after the mountain lion.
Island fun
Ohio's Lake Erie islands, like South Bass Island, are favorite summer spots for boating and ice cream.
Where it is
Lake Ontario touches New York State and the Canadian province of Ontario.
Big city
Toronto, Canada's biggest city, sits on its shore, with the tall CN Tower looking out over the water.
Small but deep
It's the smallest Great Lake by area, but it's much deeper than Lake Erie, about 800 feet at its deepest.
Ocean highway
Since 1959, the St. Lawrence Seaway has let big ocean ships sail from the Atlantic through Lake Ontario all the way to Lake Superior.
What ships carry
Ships on the Seaway carry grain, steel, salt and iron ore between the Great Lakes and the rest of the world.
Niagara
The Niagara River brings Lake Erie's water over Niagara Falls and into Lake Ontario.
Thousand Islands
Where the lake flows into the St. Lawrence River are the Thousand Islands. Thousand Island salad dressing is named after them!
Snow machine
Cold winds blowing over the lake dump huge 'lake-effect' snowfalls on nearby towns like Oswego, New York.
Its name
Its name comes from an Iroquoian word often translated as 'lake of shining waters.'
Tallest on Earth
Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, is the tallest mountain on Earth at about 29,032 feet.
Its name
Himalaya means 'home of snow' in Sanskrit, an ancient language of India.
Still growing
The Himalayas are still rising a tiny bit every year, because India keeps slowly pushing into the rest of Asia.
Sea fossils
Fossils of sea creatures have been found high up near Everest's top, because these rocks were once under an ocean!
Giant peaks
Ten of the world's 14 mountains taller than 8,000 meters are in the Himalayas.
First to the top
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary were the first people to reach the top of Everest, in 1953.
Mountain experts
The Sherpa people of Nepal are famous for guiding climbers up the highest peaks.
Water tower
Great rivers like the Ganges, the Indus and the Brahmaputra start in Himalayan glaciers, bringing water to over a billion people.
Wildlife
Snow leopards and red pandas live in the Himalayas.
Legend
Local stories tell of the yeti, a big, hairy snow creature. No one has ever proven it's real!

sahara.tagline: The biggest hot desert on Earth
facts: Super size
The Sahara is about as big as the whole United States.
Many countries
It stretches across parts of 11 countries in North Africa.
Desert desert
'Sahara' comes from the Arabic word for desert, so the 'Sahara Desert' means 'Desert Desert'!
Not just sand
Only about a quarter of the Sahara is sand dunes. The rest is gravel plains, rocky plateaus and mountains.
Green Sahara
About 6,000 to 10,000 years ago, the Sahara was green, with lakes, hippos and giraffes. Ancient rock art shows them!
Mega dunes
Some of its sand dunes are taller than a 50-story building.
Camel caravans
For hundreds of years, camel caravans crossed the Sahara carrying salt north and south, and traders swapped it for gold.
Hot and cold
Days can be scorching, but nights can get cold enough for frost, and snow has even fallen in the Algerian Sahara.
Big ears
The fennec fox lives here. Its huge ears help it hear bugs underground and stay cool.

country-egypt.tagline: Pyramids, pharaohs and the mighty Nile
facts: The Nile
Almost everyone in Egypt lives near the Nile River. Each year its floods once left rich soil for farming.
Hieroglyphs
Ancient Egyptians wrote with hieroglyphs, picture symbols. There were more than 700 of them!
Code cracked
The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, had the same message in three scripts, which helped a scholar decode hieroglyphs in 1822.
Treasure found
In 1922, Howard Carter found King Tutankhamun's tomb, packed with treasures and a famous golden mask.
The Sphinx
The Great Sphinx has a lion's body and a human head, carved from one giant piece of rock.
Cat lovers
Ancient Egyptians adored cats and honored Bastet, a goddess with the head of a cat.
Shortcut for ships
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, lets ships sail between the Mediterranean and Red Seas instead of going all the way around Africa.
Invention
Ancient Egyptians made one of the first toothpastes, using crushed salt, mint and flowers.
Big city
Cairo, the capital, is one of the biggest cities in Africa.

capital-united-states.tagline: The capital of the United States
facts: Its name
D.C. stands for 'District of Columbia.' It's named after George Washington and Christopher Columbus.
Planned city
The city was designed in 1791 by Pierre L'Enfant, with wide avenues and big circles.
Moving capital
New York and Philadelphia were the capital first. The government moved to Washington in 1800.
The White House
The White House has 132 rooms and 35 bathrooms. Every president since John Adams has lived there.
Biggest library
The Library of Congress is the biggest library in the world, with millions of books, maps and recordings.
Two colors
The Washington Monument is two shades of stone because building paused for years and new stone was used to finish it.
Cherry blossoms
In 1912, Japan gave the city 3,000 cherry trees. Their pink blooms bring a huge festival every spring.
Free fun
Most Smithsonian museums are free, including the Air and Space Museum and the National Zoo.
Five boroughs
New York City has five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island.
Old name
Before 1664 it was a Dutch town called New Amsterdam.
First capital
George Washington became the first US president here in 1789, when New York was the nation's capital.
Front door
About 12 million people arrived in America through Ellis Island in New York Harbor between 1892 and 1954.
Huge park
Central Park is bigger than the whole country of Monaco.
Subway city
Its subway has 472 stations, one of the biggest subway systems in the world.
Many voices
Hundreds of languages are spoken in New York City, more than almost anywhere on Earth.
Big Apple
The nickname 'the Big Apple' became famous in the 1920s, thanks to a newspaper writer who covered horse racing.
New Year's
A giant glowing ball has dropped in Times Square to welcome the New Year since 1907.
Tiny start
The Mississippi begins at Lake Itasca in Minnesota, where it's so small you can walk across it on stepping stones.
Long trip
It flows about 2,340 miles south to the Gulf of Mexico. A raindrop takes about 90 days to make the whole trip!
Ten states
It runs through or along 10 states, from Minnesota down to Louisiana.
Its name
Its name comes from an Ojibwe word meaning 'great river.'
Steamboat days
In the 1800s, paddle-wheel steamboats carried cotton, sugar, grain and passengers up and down the river.
Mark Twain
Author Mark Twain was a riverboat pilot. His pen name was a river call meaning the water was 12 feet deep, safe for boats.
River trucks
Today barges carry grain, coal and more. One barge can carry as much as about 70 big trucks.
Water stairs
On the upper river, 29 locks and dams work like giant water stairs to lift and lower boats.
Music river
Jazz was born in New Orleans, near the river's mouth, and blues and rock grew up along its banks.
Full name
Her official name is 'Liberty Enlightening the World.'
The designers
French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed her, and Gustave Eiffel, of the Eiffel Tower, built her iron skeleton.
Shipped in pieces
She crossed the ocean from France in about 350 pieces packed in 214 crates.
Size
She's about 151 feet tall, and about 305 feet with her base. Her index finger is 8 feet long!
Stairs
Visitors climb 354 steps to reach the crown, which has 25 windows.
Crown rays
The seven rays on her crown stand for the seven seas and seven continents.
Freedom
Broken chains lie at her feet, a symbol of freedom.
The torch
Visitors haven't been allowed up in the torch since 1916. Her original torch is now in a museum on the island.
Welcome
For millions of people arriving by ship, she was their very first sight of America.
Small town
Green Bay is the smallest city in America with a major pro sports team, about 107,000 people.
Most titles
The Packers have won 13 NFL championships, the most of any team, including four Super Bowls.
Cheeseheads
Fans proudly wear foam hats shaped like wedges of cheese, a nod to Wisconsin's famous dairy farms.
The Ice Bowl
In the 1967 championship game, called the Ice Bowl, it was about 13 degrees below zero at Lambeau Field.
Lambeau Leap
After scoring at home, players jump into the stands to celebrate with fans. It's called the Lambeau Leap.
Frozen tundra
Lambeau Field is nicknamed 'the frozen tundra' because of its freezing winter games.
Waiting list
The waiting list for season tickets is so long that families sign up babies so they might get seats one day.
Old team
Founded in 1919, they're the oldest NFL team still playing in the same town.
